title: Different Niches Let Many Kinds Share

scenes.visual: a spruce tree schematic with five bird dots and insects; the question appears
scenes.tts: Five kinds of small birds called warblers live in the same spruce forests in summer. The forests are in Maine and Vermont. All five eat mostly insects from the trees. How can so many kinds of animals share one place without running out of food?
scenes.narration: Five kinds of small birds called warblers live in the same spruce forests in summer. The forests are in Maine and Vermont. All five eat mostly insects from the trees. How can so many kinds of animals share one place without running out of food?

scenes.visual: habitat as the place (forest, pond), niche as the role; address and job
scenes.tts: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. A spruce forest is a habitat. A niche is the organism's role in its habitat. Think of the habitat as an address, and the niche as a job.
scenes.narration: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. A spruce forest is a habitat. A niche is the organism's role in its habitat. Think of the habitat as an address, and the niche as a job.

scenes.visual: four parts of a niche, then squirrel and earthworm in one oak forest with different niches
scenes.tts: A niche is more than one job. It includes what the organism eats, and where and when it feeds. It includes the space it uses, and what eats it. Take a Virginia oak forest. A gray squirrel and an earthworm both live there. The squirrel eats acorns and nuts. The earthworm eats dead leaves and soil. They share a habitat, but their niches are very different.

scenes.visual: resource chips; food dots shrink and the search circle grows
scenes.tts: A resource is something a living thing needs and takes from its habitat. Food, water, shelter and space are resources. Part of an organism's niche is how it gets them. When food runs short, an animal may have to search more places. So a niche can shift.

scenes.visual: two niche circles overlap a lot, then apart; red competition bar grows then shrinks
scenes.tts: A species is one kind of living thing. When two species need the same limited resource, they compete. Competition is a struggle for resources that are in short supply. If two species have niches that overlap a lot and the resource they share is in short supply, they compete a lot. One may get most of the food, and the other may do poorly. If their niches are different, they compete less.

scenes.visual: one habitat holding five different niche ovals with small overlaps; biodiversity label; answer line
scenes.tts: So how can so many kinds of animals share one place? Different niches help. Species that use a habitat in different ways compete less. That lets more kinds of living things share one place. The variety of living things in a place is called biodiversity. Using a place differently does not remove all competition. But it helps.
